title: Urine & Respiratory Specimen Culture Workflow

references.label: CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

purpose: To process urine and respiratory specimens for culture using quantitative (urine) and specimen-quality-screened (respiratory) approaches suited to sources that normally carry some resident flora.
principle: Because urine and the respiratory tract (outside the lower airway) are not sterile in the same sense as blood, both workflows use additional steps — quantitative culture for urine, and specimen quality screening for sputum — to help separate clinically significant growth from expected background flora or poor-quality sampling.
requiredMaterials: Sputum specimen container with quality-assessment capability (e.g. Gram stain screen)

procedure.note: The calibrated loop's volume is method/manufacturer-specific and is the basis for reporting colony-forming units per mL, not a universal fixed reading.
procedure.instruction: For urine: use a calibrated loop (e.g. a defined-volume loop, per the laboratory's method) to inoculate a measured volume onto appropriate media, enabling a quantitative colony count rather than a simple presence/absence result.

For urine: incubate and, after growth, calculate approximate colony count per mL from the number of colonies and the loop's calibrated volume; correlate against the laboratory's significance threshold for the collection method used (clean-catch vs. catheterized vs. suprapubic thresholds differ).

procedure.note: A specimen dominated by squamous epithelial cells is often rejected or reported as unsuitable for culture, per the laboratory's quality-screening criteria — this criterion is method-defined, not a single number applicable everywhere.
procedure.instruction: For sputum/respiratory specimens: first assess specimen quality by Gram stain screening (squamous epithelial cells vs. white blood cells per low-power field) to judge whether the sample represents lower respiratory secretions or is contaminated with oral flora.
For sputum/respiratory specimens judged acceptable, culture on appropriate media and interpret growth relative to expected respiratory flora and the specific pathogens being sought.
Report both urine and respiratory results with the context needed for interpretation: colony count and organism(s) for urine; specimen quality grade and organism(s) for respiratory.

observations: Urine: colony count and organism identity. Respiratory: specimen quality grade, predominant organism(s), and correlation with Gram stain screening.
interpretation: Urine colony counts are compared against collection-method-specific significance thresholds rather than a single universal number; respiratory culture results are only as meaningful as the specimen quality that produced them, which is why the quality screen is performed first.
precautions: Use a properly calibrated loop and consistent technique for urine to keep quantitative counts reproducible.
Do not skip the respiratory specimen quality screen — culturing and reporting from a clearly contaminated specimen can mislead clinical decisions.
limitations: Quantitative urine thresholds and respiratory quality-screening criteria are standard-method-dependent and vary by the laboratory's adopted criteria and the collection method used.
biosafetyNotes: Standard precautions apply; use a biosafety cabinet for aerosol-generating manipulation of respiratory specimens where risk of an aerosol-transmissible pathogen is plausible.
